profile.reading:
The New York Stock Exchange's primary data center sits on North Central Avenue in Mahwah, Bergen County, New Jersey. It is now owned and operated by Intercontinental Exchange, Inc. (NYSE: ICE), which acquired NYSE Euronext for approximately 8.2 billion dollars in a deal announced in December 2012 and completed the following year.

The Mahwah facility was built around five 20,000 square foot modular data halls, totaling roughly 100,000 square feet of raised floor space, inside a building with an overall footprint of about 400,000 square feet. Total power capacity is reported at 28 megawatts. The modules were brought online in stages over roughly two years in the period leading up to the ICE acquisition, as part of a broader consolidation of NYSE's technology footprint.

Before Mahwah, NYSE's trading and market data infrastructure was spread across eight data centers, six in the United States and two in Europe. The Mahwah build, alongside a companion site in Basildon, England, let the exchange shrink to two primary production data centers serving its global markets. Mahwah houses the electronic matching engines that execute trades on the New York Stock Exchange and other markets ICE operates, and it doubles as a colocation facility, renting rack and cage space to proprietary trading firms, market makers and brokers who want their servers physically close to the matching engines to minimize network latency. This low latency colocation business is a specialized niche within the data center industry, distinct from the general enterprise or cloud colocation offered by most commercial providers, and it has made Mahwah one of the most closely watched facilities in electronic trading since it opened.

Today the site operates under ICE's colocation and connectivity business, marketed as ICE Global Network and Colocation, which publishes technical specifications, cabinet options and network access details for prospective trading firms directly on its own site rather than through third party listing services. The facility's profile has made it a recurring subject of financial and technology press coverage, particularly around latency, market structure and high frequency trading, since the physical location of a trading firm's servers inside the Mahwah building can measurably affect execution speed relative to competitors.

Public information about Mahwah is unusually detailed for a data center, a reflection of ICE's own published specifications for its colocation customers rather than third party estimation. Granular operational details such as current tenant occupancy or specific future expansion plans beyond the original five module build are not published.

reading:
This row is recorded under the lower case operator string nyse, which comes straight from an OpenStreetMap tag rather than from any company. The building is the New York Stock Exchange's primary data centre in Mahwah, Bergen County, New Jersey, and the entity that owns and runs it today is Intercontinental Exchange, which acquired NYSE Euronext for approximately 8.2 billion dollars in a transaction announced on 19 December 2012 and completed the following year.

The securities filings settle the timeline that trade coverage left vague. NYSE Euronext's annual report for 2012 states that the company launched two new data centres, in Basildon, England and Mahwah, New Jersey, in 2011, that all matching engines for its European markets were consolidated at Basildon and its United States securities exchanges migrated to Mahwah, and that its information services and technology segment benefited from colocation services offered at both sites. The two buildings replaced an earlier estate of eight data centres, six in the United States and two in Europe. Because colocation at Mahwah is a service of a registered national securities exchange rather than a purely commercial arrangement, its existence and its economics surface in exchange filings in a way that ordinary colocation contracts never do.

The operator's own published technical specification for the site, issued under the ICE Global Network and Colocation brand, gives the address as 1700 McArthur Boulevard, Mahwah, New Jersey 07430, in a 398,000 square foot building on a 28 acre site 34 miles from Wall Street. It states 28 megawatts of total site electrical power, Tier 4 guided design of all critical infrastructure at 2N or N plus 2, 48 hours of emergency generator fuel and cooling tower water at full load, and double action pre action sprinkler fire suppression. Colocation space is described as scalable to 20,000 square feet at 150 watts per square foot, and cabinets are sold in roughly 4 kilowatt, 8 kilowatt and 12 to 15 kilowatt configurations, each fed by dual branch circuits from separate distribution paths.

Those numbers must not be collapsed into one another. The 28 megawatts is total site electrical power, the service the building can draw, and it covers cooling, losses and everything else alongside the servers. The published density of 150 watts per square foot across a 20,000 square foot hall works out near 3 megawatts of IT load per hall, so the design capacity of the colocation floors is materially below the site figure. A registry entry that reports 28 megawatts as the exchange's IT capacity is reporting the wrong quantity, and the operator has published no separate critical IT load total.

The site also publishes network detail that a general purpose colocation provider would have no reason to disclose, including two autonomous system numbers, 64552 for its liquidity centre network and 26585 for its high availability service, along with BGP hold and keepalive timers, connector and optical standards for each port speed, and a policy of rate limiting liquidity centre ports to ten percent of port speed. That level of published specificity follows from what is actually being sold here, which is measured proximity to the matching engines rather than floor space, and from the fact that firms buying it need identical, auditable conditions.

One registry side note applies. The stored street value on this row is a reverse geocode to North Central Avenue, a nearest road answer rather than a verified address, and the operator's own specification gives McArthur Boulevard, a street more commonly rendered as MacArthur Boulevard in local usage. The stored coordinates fall within a short distance of the published address.
